Setting up the consent prompt

Nine taps, once. After that every consent conversation you record with Nabla comes out in the same six sections.

Before you start

You need Nabla Copilot on your phone, signed in with your UIHC account, and the prompt below. The prompt is also on its own page with four full example notes; both links are at the foot of this page.

The nine taps

  1. Shown as a generalized recreation.

  2. Shown as a generalized recreation.

  5. Shown as a generalized recreation.

  9. Shown as a generalized recreation.

Nine taps. Once. Never again.

The prompt

 TASK

   Generate a PRE-ANESTHESIA EVALUATION NOTE based on the conversation.


 GOALS

   Reflect a clear, attentive, and patient-centered interaction.

   Demonstrate that risks, plan, and next steps were thoroughly discussed.

   Maintain concise, structured, and clinically accurate documentation.


 STYLE

   Professional but warm tone.

   Avoid robotic or generic phrasing.

   When appropriate, briefly incorporate relevant human elements from the conversation,
   for example the patient’s day, the weather, or small personal context, to reflect rapport.

   Do not state that anything is “by protocol”.




 STRUCTURE

  01     INTERACTION SUMMARY

           Brief narrative of the encounter.
           Include the patient’s concerns, preferences, or expectations.

           Include any relevant personal or contextual details the patient mentioned.

           Include evidence of engagement: questions asked, comfort level, participation.
           Avoid generic descriptors such as “warm” or “pleasant”. Show the interaction
           through content.

           Prefer concrete details from the conversation over generic statements.
           When the patient expresses a preference, for example same day discharge, reflect
           that the team acknowledged it and folded it into planning.
    02    ANESTHESIA PLAN

            Clearly describe the planned anesthesia technique or techniques.
            Reflect personalization based on the patient’s condition and the procedure.

            Include the IV plan only where it is relevant.


    03    RISKS DISCUSSED

            Clearly and explicitly list the anesthesia related risks discussed.

            Include both common and serious risks where the conversation raised them.

            Use clear and understandable language.


    04    PATIENT UNDERSTANDING AND CONSENT

            Document that the clinician explained risks, benefits, and alternatives.

            Document that the patient demonstrated understanding.
            Document that the patient had the opportunity to ask questions.

            Document that the clinician addressed all questions.

            Document that the patient agrees with the plan.


    05    EXPECTATIONS AND NEXT STEPS

            Describe what happens next in the perioperative flow: IV placement where needed,
            transfer to the operating room, monitoring, induction or sedation, and the recovery
            phases including PACU.

            Include expectations the conversation covered, for example pain control, nausea,
            and the recovery process.


    06    ADDITIONAL RELEVANT POINTS

            Include any other clinically relevant details the conversation covered.
            Avoid unnecessary repetition or filler.

From a conversation to a note

  1. Find your patient. Haiku, Hyperspace, either one.
  2. Launch Nabla from inside the chart. A tab in Epic or a button in Haiku.
  3. Check the one line summary. It comes from Evidently.
  4. Start the encounter.
  5. Finish it. The note is generated for you.
  6. Open the consent, fill it as you always do, and import the note with .nabla at the end. The dot phrase pulls in the encounter with the six section structure.

Six steps, and five of them you already do.

Two things to remember

  • Nabla keeps an encounter for 14 days. The app says it in its own words: "Nabla saves your encounters for 14 days. Remember to copy them into your EHR."
  • The generated section appends to the institutional consent note. The template stays the legal backbone of the record. You read the draft, correct it, and sign it.

How we use it safely

  • The patient agrees before recording starts. The anesthesiologist asks permission to use a hospital approved AI tool for note taking, and the patient agrees before the scribe begins.
  • The anesthesiologist reviews and edits every draft. A clinician reads the generated note, corrects it, and signs it. The AI drafts; the physician remains the author.
  • The institutional consent template stays intact. The generated section appends to the required consent note. The template remains the legal backbone of the record.
